text: Encryption shows up at three different points in a data's lifecycle, and a mature program needs all three. This lesson focuses on SQL Server's real T-SQL for protecting data at rest, plus the one approach that protects data even from the database administrator.

At rest, data sitting in a database file or backup, protected so a stolen file can't be read without the key. In transit, data moving across a network, protected by TLS. In use, data actively being processed in memory, the hardest of the three, and the newest area of active development.

Transparent Data Encryption protects an entire database at rest, transparently, applications don't notice. It's a chain: a master key protects a certificate, the certificate protects a database encryption key, and that key actually encrypts the data pages. Back up the certificate immediately, without it, an encrypted database becomes permanently unreadable, even to the organization that encrypted it.

Sometimes encrypting the whole database is more than the job calls for. Cell-level encryption protects one column, using a symmetric key protected by a certificate. ENCRYPTBYKEY writes an encrypted value, DECRYPTBYKEY reads it back once the key is open. Unlike a token, this is genuinely reversible, the ciphertext mathematically encodes the original value, and anyone who opens the right key gets it back.

Both TDE and cell-level encryption decrypt inside the database engine, meaning a database administrator with enough access can still potentially see plaintext. Always Encrypted moves encryption and decryption to the client driver, outside the engine entirely. The database stores and processes only ciphertext, never the key or plaintext, so even a sysadmin querying the column directly sees only encrypted bytes.

That's the strongest guarantee in SQL Server's encryption toolkit, solving a real segregation-of-duties problem the other two don't. Next up: key management, the piece every one of these techniques actually depends on.
